name: Warrior II
hero_alt: Warrior II, seen from the side
meta_description: Front knee not reaching 90°, back knee bending, torso leaning, arms drooping? Five things usually hold back Warrior II, and a daily exercise that fixes each one.
og_description: Five things usually hold back Warrior II, and a daily exercise that fixes each one.
lede: Front knee over the ankle at a right angle, back leg straight, torso upright, arms level. Here’s the rubric Posewise measures it against, and what to train when you miss.
rubric_intro: Posewise checks eight things, from the side and the front. Here’s what good looks like.

rubric.name: Front knee
rubric.good: Bent to a right angle, over the ankle

rubric.name: Knee tracking
rubric.good: Over your front foot, not caving in

rubric.name: Shoulders
rubric.good: Level, not tipping toward the front leg

fixes.outcome: your front knee will reach a 90° bend.
fixes.why: The shape is there, the depth isn’t. That points to leg strength, not technique.
fixes.cue: Sink until your front thigh is parallel to the floor, knee over ankle.

fixes.outcome: your front knee will track over your toes.
fixes.why: When the outer glutes are weak, the front knee caves in toward the big toe.
fixes.cue: Press your front knee out toward your little toe.

fixes.action: Lengthen your inner thighs and quads
fixes.why: Tight groin and quad muscles pull the back knee into a bend.
fixes.cue: Press the outer edge of your back foot down and straighten the leg.

fixes.outcome: your torso will stay stacked between your feet.
fixes.why: When the trunk gives way under load, it leans toward the front leg and one shoulder drops.
fixes.cue: Stack your shoulders over your hips.

fixes.outcome: your arms will stay level with your shoulders.
fixes.why: Drooping arms are shoulder endurance running out, not a flexibility problem.
fixes.cue: Reach out through your fingertips, shoulders soft.

cues: And two cues: point your front foot straight ahead, and turn your head to look out over your front hand.

faq.q: How deep should my front knee bend in Warrior II?
faq.a: About 90°, with your front thigh close to parallel to the floor and your knee stacked over your ankle. If you can’t get there, lengthen your stance.

faq.q: Should my front knee go past my toes?
faq.a: No. Keep it over your ankle and pointing toward your second and third toes. If it drifts past your toes, step your feet wider apart.

faq.q: Why do my arms get tired in Warrior II?
faq.a: Holding your arms at shoulder height is endurance work for the shoulders. Keep reaching through your fingertips and let your shoulders stay relaxed; it gets easier with practice.

faq.q: Where should I look in Warrior II?
faq.a: Turn your head to look out over your front middle finger, keeping your neck long.

faq.q: How can I check my Warrior II form at home?
faq.a: Film yourself from the side and the front. Or use Posewise, an iPhone app that measures your Warrior II with the camera, speaks corrections as you hold it, and builds a six-minute daily plan for what it finds.

llms_summary: the five things that usually hold back Warrior II (leg strength for a 90° front knee, outer-hip strength for knee tracking, tight groin and quads bending the back leg, core strength for an upright torso, shoulder endurance for level arms), with the alignment rubric and a daily exercise for each.
